label: text
text: [The Wimbledon championship commence on Monday, June 22.] WHO THEY ARE.

label: text
text: Of America's 1925 Wimbledon team, A. Wallis Myers, C.B.E., writes:—

label: text
text: The six American players who are coming to Wimbledon in June to play an international match against England and to compete in the championships will, with two exceptions, be making their debut in this country. They are a young, post-war team, and their advent in our midst is another proof of the United States Association's desire, by an interchange of players, to strengthen the ties of friendship.

label: text
text: Charles (“Chuck”) S. Garland is the oldest member of the team, and will lead it. He was here in 1920 with the American Davis Cup team which beat England and France. In partnership with R. N. Williams he won the doubles championship at the old Wimbledon, defeating Tilden and Johnston in the semifinal, and Paike and Kingscote in the final. Pressure of business in Pittsburgh kept Garland out of the game for two years after his return to America, but he is now resident in New York, and has made a welcome reappearance on court. John Henmessey, hailing from Chicago, is one of the Middle West players, trained on "dirt" courts, who have sprung to the front in the last year or two. He beat G. L. Patterson and B. I. C. Norton in his own district last summer, and at Forest Hills in September was responsible for Jean Borotra's defeat in the America championship. He is ranked No. 7 in his own country.

label: text
text: Ray - Casey, like Johnston and McLoughlin, has emerged from the golden gate of the West. He is ranked No. 2. in California, and won the doubles championship of Mexico with Vincent Richards last year, the pair defeating the brothers Kinsey; the present doubles champions of America. He has a powerful service and a smash almost as violent. Lucien Williams, a former captain of Yale, and ranked No. 11 in the national list, visited England with the Yale and Harvard University team in 1922. He is now the third best player in the Middle West, coming next to Hennessy and George Lott, the U.S.A. junior champion. Of Lawrence B. Rice, the New England player, Tilden has always held a high opinion. He was No. 9 in America in 1921 and No. 11 in 1922. At present he is No. 15, but his opportunities for play have been restricted by business ties, and he may very well shine over here as brightly as any of his fellows.

label: text
text: The American team will probably compete in the French national championships at St. Cloud before coming to Wimbledon. The majority of them have learnt and developed their game on non-turf courts; they will indeed, be more at home on the Paris courts than at Wimbledon. They may not contain a Wimbledon winner among them, yet they are all products of the modern, aggressive, quickfooted school, and their presence at Wimbledon is sure to provide a stimulus—and possibly a surprise.

label: text
text: Last week's results were about as expected, although. Taikoo managed a wonderful victory against the Dock Club, I understand that with two rinks finished and the third rink only two heads to go, Taikoo wanted nine to win. They laid a five and a four and thus pulled the game out of the fire, scoring an almost impossible victory.

label: text
text: .The Bowling Green Club decisively defeated〉the Cricket Club, whilst Craigengower retain their position at the head of the league by a fine victory over the Civil Service on the latter's green.

label: text
text: The Police, by defeating the Taikoo second string by a substantial margin, retain their unbeaten record in the second division. They seem almost certain to gain promotion at the end of the season. Playing with a very weakened team at Sookumpoo, the Kowloon Cricket Club were overwhelmed by the Indians, whilst at East Point the home team secured their first win at the expense of the Yacht Club.

label: text
text: From a visit paid to the various greens in the Coolny it seems that none has suffered any special damage from the very heavy rains. The Civil Service green had a marvellous escape, thanks to the high banking around it. The Police-green has a little mud on it but this should be cleared in time for their next home game.

label: text
text: Of the games to be played in the first division, that between the Civil Service and Taikoo would appear to be the most interesting, for the home team will need to win to save themselves from relegation, whilst the visitors will try hard for the two points to keep them in the running for the championship.

label: text

label: text

label: text
text: In the second division, Taikoo should dispose of the East Point team. I understand the K.C.C. team will be considerably weakened by the absence of some of their best players to-morrow and the Yacht Club might, with a slice of luck, pick up two valuable points.

label: text
text: The Police are visiting the Indians' ground with a firm determination to lower the home team's undefeated (home) record. label: paragraph_title
text: Peking, June 18.

label: text
text: Despite official statements that every effort would be made to prevent anti-foreign riots, nothing is being done to hinder dangerous inflammatory agitation.

label: text
text: Thousands of incendiary and provocative posters have been posted up throughout Peking, this morning, depicting British police shooting and bayonetting defenceless students, women and children lying on the ground.

label: text
text: While thus stirring up the masses, students and other educated Chinese refuse to face the real facts.

label: text
text: Mr. Palaret H.B.M. Chargé d'Affaires, unofficially offered to see the student deputation and explain the British point of view, but the offer was refused. The vernacular papers are mostly refusing to print Reuter telegrams. They are inserting an absurdly garbled version of events. For example: The Japanese at Hankow are alleged to have injured each other; the foreign buildings at Kiukiang caught fire themselves; while the Yi Ship Pao asserts that Mr. Mackenzie died of sickness and that the British Consul ordered the doctor to mutilate the remains and then accused the Chinese of murder.

label: paragraph_title
text: Negotiations Broken Off.

label: text
text: The diplomatic commission has broken off negotiations, owing to the divergence of Chinese and Foreign views.

label: text
text: The commission, sent to Shanghai by representatives of the interested Powers in order to investigate recent events and endeavour to find an immediate solution of the difficulties which were the direct outcome of those events, met the Chinese delegates to day for the third time, at the office of the Commissioner for Foreign Affairs.

label: text
text: At this meeting, the commission handed to the Chinese delegation certain concrete proposals which in their opinion, constituted a fair basis for settlement.

label: text
text: The Chinese delegation presented, once again to the commission a series of demands, which had no direct connection with the recent regrettable occurrences, although the commission had been careful to emphasise from the very start that it had not been authorised to deal with these points.

label: text
text: The Chinese delegation intimately, moreover, that these points must be dealt with at the same time as the incidents themselves.

label: paragraph_title
text: Shanghai, June 18.

label: text
text: It is to be noted that the instructions given to the commission are based on the Note, addressed to the Legations by the Waichiaopu, in which mention only is made of four points, all of which are directly connected with the incidents themselves.

label: text
text: Under the circumstances, these two points of view would seem to be altogether too divergent to admit of any hope of an early solution on the spot; and the commission has, in consequence, decided to leave for Peking tonight.

label: text
text:
The previous message was an official translation of the French text of the communiqué on the matter. The commission entrains to night; and the whole question, therefore, goes back to Peking.
It is understood the Chinese delegation to-day presented the whole thirteen original demands, including the rendition of the Mixed Court; the dismissal of the Secretary of the Municipal Council and that municipal franchise be given to the Chinese.

label: text
text: In each of three cases of robbery or attempted robbery heard yesterday at the Criminal Sessions the prisoners owed their appearance to the plucky conduct of the women of the households whom probably they had looked upon as easy victims.

label: text
text: Escaping from her bonds and ungagging herself a woman at Shanghai Street, Mongkoktsui, pursued one of the robbers who had taken jewellery from the house. Her action led to his arrest and he was sentenced to five years' imprisonment.

label: text
text: One of four women playing dominoes in a house at Chatham Road, Hunghom, when robbers rushed in and presented revolvers had the pluck to defy them and run to the verandah blowing a police whistle. The intending robbers immediately decamped but one was captured by Mr. Fokin, of Alex Ross and Co., who was passing by.

label: text
text: The captured man was sentenced to five years' imprisonment.

label: text
text: The spirited resistance of a woman at Shamshuipo scared other robbers who entered a house in Ki Lung Street, and they decamped without taking anything. A Chinese living on the bottom floor grappled with one of them and managed to detain him until the police arrived and he also was sentenced to five years' imprisonment.

label: paragraph_title
text: MOTORIST CHARGED.

label: paragraph_title
text: MR. WERSCHKUL'S EVENING RIDE.

label: paragraph_title
text: REPULSE HAY INCIDENTS.

label: text
text: The greater part of three hours was taken up at the Central Magistracy yesterday afternoon with the hearing of the case against Mr. Howard T. Werschkul, a young American flour broker, who was charged with causing bodily harm to an Indian watchman in the employ of the Repulse Bay Hotel by wanton and furious driving.

label: text
text: The case for the Crown was that he drove a car in a zigzag course past the entrance to the Hotel on the night of Saturday, June 6, that he had not full control of the car and that as a result he knocked down the watchman who was standing outside the Hotel.

label: text
text: Witnesses called all attributed to the defendant's car a dangerous speed for such a spot. Mr. F. G. H. Haslam, who watched the car's progress from the main flight of steps leading up to the Hotel while he was waiting for his own car, said that the occupants were laughing and singing. The car was zigzagging along the road at a speed of about 20-25 miles an hour. He did not see the watchman but heard the crash. The car did not stop. Mr. M. M. Maas, of the A.P.C. gave corroborative evidence.

label: text
text: Mr. C. Edwards, of the Hongkong and Shanghai Bank, who was waiting at the foot of the steps to the Hotel in the main road said that the car was travelling at considerable speed and cut in on another car in such a manner that it caused simultaneous exclamations of surprise from himself and others who were with him. He should think it was going at 18 miles an hour when it passed the Hotel.

label: text
text: Mr A. Grimmett, of the Revenue Office, who was outside the Hotel at the time at the top of the steps said that he thought the car was going to run over the spot where he and his wife were standing. He pushed his wife out of the way and jumped clear himself. The car swerved and hit the watchman on the opposite side. Witness called to the driver to stop but the latter took no notice. The car was going at about 25 miles an hour in his opinion. He noticed that the number was 175.

label: text
text: Mr. Graham, of the Colonial Secretariat, said that the Indian watchman seeing his danger jumped in an attempt to get clear but was caught and carried for some yards.

label: text
text: The injuries sustained were a fractured thigh bone and abrasions, said Dr. W. L. Paterson.

label: text
text: The case for the Crown having been closed the defendant went into the witness box.

label: text
text: On the night in question he had dinner with some friends, among whom were M. Dupre, the boxer, and after watching the dancers it was suggested that they should go for a ride. They got as far as the Hotel garage in the car when it was found that no one had any cigarettes so they returned. On driving off again witness (who was driving) felt something strike the front of the car but thought they had struck the rail. Later when they stopped for a puncture near Tytam Tuk reservoir they found that the front head light had been broken and that it was no longer functioning. At Shaukiwan they were stopped by a police officer who told them he had been warned to keep a lookout for a car of their number.

label: text
text: Mr. Werschkul said that the first drink of an alcoholic nature he had on the day in question was a cocktail or two before dinner. He was going at a speed of fifteen miles, an hour at the time he passed the Hotel which he admitted was faster than he ought to have been travelling at that spot. When he drove down the hill after returning to procure the cigarettes the car was in first gear and he changed into second at the bottom as he took the turn to approach the hotel for the second time.

label: text
text: Mr. Andre Dupre gave corrosive evidence and said that in his opinion the car was travelling at a speed of about ten miles or fifteen kilometres an hour.

label: text
text: The case was adjourned until this afternoon.

label: text
text: The Coroner's Inquiry into the death of a coolie as the result of a motor car running into the pavement at West Point, which, as stated yesterday, opened at the Central Magistracy, concluded in the afternoon when a verdict of manslaughter against the driver was returned. A warrant is out for the arrest of the driver, Fun Pulang, who is absconded whilst on bail of $5,000.
